item.title: Nvidia in talks to give credit support for Nscale's deal with Anthropic
item.description: Nvidia is reportedly considering billions of dollars in credit guarantees to help Nscale finance a West Virginia AI data centre for Anthropic, though the deal has not been finalised.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Nvidia is in talks to offer AI cloud provider Nscale billions of dollars in credit guarantees to support debt funding for a data center earmarked for Anthropic, The Information reported on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the talks. The credit support would help fund power infrastructure and construction of Nscale's AI data centre in West Virginia, which Anthropic plans to use, according to the report. Nvidia is an investor in the UK-based cloud provider. The deal has not been signed and terms could still change, the report said. Nvidia, Nscale and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Claude maker Anthropic struck a deal in August to spend $45 billion to rent computing power from Nscale's West Virginia data center campus. Nscale is also in talks to sell about 460 megawatts of AI computing power to Anthropic in another deal that could also be worth about $45 billion. The report comes as companies such as CoreWeave and Firmus, which are both backed by Nvidia, have been hit by concerns about debt financing behind the AI build-out.

Sebi imposes ₹1 crore fine on CDSL for multiple compliance lapses Regulator flags shortcomings in pledge-rejection communication, cybersecurity controls, vulnerability patching and disaster recovery drills

Sebi imposes a Rs 1 crore penalty on CDSL over multiple compliance and cybersecurity lapses. (Photo: Reuters)

PTI New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 11:11 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Markets regulator Sebi on Friday imposed a penalty of Rs 1 crore on Central Depository Services (India) Ltd (CDSL) for multiple compliance lapses, including failure to communicate reasons for rejection of pledge requests to the depository participants (DPs) of both the pledgor and pledgee and shortcomings in disaster recovery drills. CDSL has been directed to pay the penalty within 45 days, failing which recovery proceedings may be initiated. In its 102-page order, Sebi said CDSL had violated several regulatory requirements during FY2023-24, following an inspection of its operations. The violations included failure to communicate reasons for rejection of pledge requests to the depository participants of both the pledgor and pledgee, non-compliance with prescribed procedures for handling Client Unpaid Securities Accounts (CUSA), inadequate measures to prevent unauthorised data transmission and shortcomings in disaster recovery operations.

The regulator also found that CDSL had failed to patch identified vulnerabilities within the timeline prescribed by Sebi. Further, its Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) exercise was not comprehensive as it did not cover all domains and external applications. "Noticee has been found to have committed multiple compliance lapses in the discharge of its depository functions. These include failure to communicate the reasons for rejection of pledge requests to the DPs of the pledgor and pledgee, non-adherence to the joint proposal framed ...in relation to CUSA operations, inadequate measures to prevent unauthorised transmission of data, incomplete migration of operations to the DR site during the DR drill, failure to patch vulnerabilities within the timeline stipulated by Sebi, and conducting a VAPT exercise that was not comprehensive," Sebi said.

In July, the regulator imposed a penalty of Rs 1 crore on CDSL for cybersecurity lapses linked to the malware attack that disrupted its systems in November 2022.   4 firms get Sebi nod for IPO   Four companies — home appliances maker Atomberg Technologies, organised food and grocery retailer Ratnadeep Retail, construction and infrastructure firm GNI Infrastructure and liquid carbon dioxide (CO2) producer Punjab Carbonic — have secured the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (Sebi’s) approval to raise funds through initial public offerings (IPOs).   These firms filed their preliminary IPO papers between March and August. After reviewing their draft papers, the regulator gave its final observation during October 27-30, an update from the markets regulator showed on Friday. Sebi’s observations mark an important step in the IPO process, allowing companies to proceed with the preparations for their public issues, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.   According to the draft red herring prospectus (DRHP), Atomberg’s IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of 76.5 million equity shares. As a part of the OFS, A91 Partners, Temasekbacked V-Sciences Investments, Jungle Ventures, Inflexor, Steadview Capital Mauritius and Survam Partners LLP will offload their shares.   Ratnadeep Retail’s IPO comprises a fresh issue of equity shares aggregating up to ₹400 crore and an OFS of nearly 14.9 million equity shares by promoters. GNI Infrastructure’s proposed IPO will be a combination of a fresh issue of 21 million shares and an OFS of 93.88 lakh shares by promoters and existing shareholders, according to the draft papers.   Punjab Carbonic’s proposed IPO is a combination of a fresh issue of 6 million equity shares and an OFS of 3.5 million equity shares.   Meanwhile, the draft IPO papers of WOG Technologies were withdrawn/returned on October 30, as per an update  with Sebi.

item.title: Sideloading on Android: What Google's new rules mean for rival app stores
item.description: Google's new Registered App Stores programme promises easier app installs and background updates for rival marketplaces on Android. But will it improve competition with Google Play?
item.dc:creator: Harsh Shivam
item.content:encoded: Google has opened enrollment for its Registered App Stores programme, which will allow approved third-party app marketplaces to install applications with a single tap and deliver updates in the background on supported Android devices from December 1. The programme gives alternative app stores a more direct route to reach Android users, but access to these features will depend on meeting Google's verification, security and operational requirements. The move does not introduce third-party app stores to Android. Users have been able to download alternative marketplaces such as Epic Games Store and F-Droid, or install applications directly through APK files, outside Google Play. However, these installations typically involve additional system prompts, manual permissions and separate confirmation for app updates.ALSO READ: WhatsApp adds group status, permanent pins, unread message filters and moreGoogle's new programme changes this installation process for marketplaces that qualify. Registered stores will be able to install apps without secondary system confirmation screens, while updates can be downloaded and installed in the background, subject to user settings. Users will also receive notifications about download progress and installation status. The programme is optional. Marketplaces that do not register can continue distributing applications through Android, although their installation experience will remain unchanged.What changes under Google's Registered App Stores programme?Under Android's existing sideloading process, users installing an alternative app store must allow it to install unknown applications through system settings. Each subsequent app installation also requires a separate confirmation. Updates distributed through these stores require user approval. Registered App Stores will receive permission to install applications directly through the Android system once the marketplace has been verified. This removes the additional confirmation screens for individual installations. The programme also allows registered marketplaces to manage app updates in the background, with users retaining control over automatic updates. However, registration is not an automatic approval for unrestricted app distribution. Google requires marketplaces to operate as legitimate, open platforms that allow eligible developers to distribute applications under clear and non-discriminatory policies. They must provide users with information about applications, including developer details, version information, download size and relevant safety disclosures. Marketplaces must also allow users to uninstall applications through the same listing or management page used to install them, support app restoration and archiving, and provide a mechanism to update the marketplace itself. There are financial and technical requirements as well. Ars Technica reported that the fee is $10,000 a year, with additional review charges possible if a store's catalogue exceeds Google's malware threshold.ALSO READ: Alphabet loses over $500 billion in market value as AI hits Google searchApplicants must register as organisations through the Android Developer Console, complete developer verification and establish ownership of their marketplace's package name. They must also submit their store's APK for malware scanning and provide Google with their complete app catalogue and subsequent updates for security review. Google can remove a marketplace from the programme if it fails to meet these requirements. However, the company states that registered stores remain responsible for their catalogues and that Google will not moderate the content distributed through them. The programme will be available from December 1, 2026, on devices running Android 17 QPR2 or later in supported regions, including India. It is not currently available in the US. The rollout will therefore depend on both regional availability and whether device manufacturers deliver the required Android update. Android Developers Ars TechnicaWhy is Google formalising third-party app stores?The programme is part of Google's broader changes to Android's app distribution and billing policies following its legal dispute with Epic Games, the developer of Fortnite. Epic sued Google in 2020, arguing that the company used its control over Android and Google Play to restrict competition in app distribution and in-app payments. In 2023, a US jury found Google had maintained an illegal monopoly in the Android app distribution and billing markets. A subsequent court injunction required Google to make changes that would allow competing app stores to reach Android users and compete with Google Play. Google challenged the ruling, but the legal dispute continued through subsequent proceedings. In November 2025, the companies announced a proposed settlement, followed by a revised agreement in March 2026. The changes included alternative billing options, lower service fees and a programme for registered third-party app stores. Google's March announcement presented the registration framework as a way to make alternative app stores easier to install while retaining security checks. Epic welcomed the changes, saying they would allow competing marketplaces to operate on Android and give developers more distribution options. However, the US rollout has a separate legal complication. Google and Epic's revised settlement requires court approval. Google has indicated that the Registered App Stores programme will initially operate outside the US, with its US availability dependent on the legal process. Google has also introduced separate arrangements for third-party stores to access Google Play's app catalogue in the US. The distinction is important because the registration programme is not a court-mandated requirement for every third-party store. It is a voluntary framework through which marketplaces can obtain additional Android system capabilities.Does Google become a gatekeeper for alternative app distribution?The registration framework raises questions about how much control Google should have over competing marketplaces on an operating system that has traditionally allowed users to install software from outside its official app store. Google's security requirements have a clear purpose. Requiring developer verification, malware scanning and regular catalogue checks can make it harder for malicious applications to circulate through third-party stores. Users also benefit from having fewer installation prompts and a more consistent update process. However, the programme creates a distinction between marketplaces that receive Google's approval and those that continue to operate outside the framework. While the latter can still distribute applications, they do not get the same installation and update capabilities. The requirement to share an entire app catalogue and subsequent updates with Google also gives the company visibility into applications distributed through competing stores. Google says this information is needed for malware review, while marketplaces remain responsible for their own content. The annual fee and organisational verification requirements could also prove difficult for smaller independent marketplaces. There is a further question about how Google will assess applications and enforce its requirements. The programme allows Google to suspend a store's registered status if it fails to meet the prescribed standards. Although this does not prevent the marketplace from continuing to operate through conventional sideloading, losing registration would mean losing the simplified installation experience. This makes the registration process an important point of control over how easily rival marketplaces can reach users, even if Google does not have exclusive authority over app distribution on Android.How does Google's approach compare with Apple's alternative app stores?Apple's approach to alternative app distribution offers a useful comparison, although the circumstances behind the changes are different. Unlike Android, Apple's iOS ecosystem traditionally did not allow users to install third-party app marketplaces. Developers had to distribute applications through the App Store, subject to Apple's review and commercial terms. Regulatory intervention forced Apple to change this model in the European Union under the Digital Markets Act (DMA). Starting with iOS 17.4 in March 2024, Apple allowed authorised alternative app marketplaces to distribute applications in the region. Developers can also distribute applications through their websites under certain conditions. Apple retains a verification process for marketplace operators and requires applications distributed outside the App Store to undergo notarisation. This is a baseline security review intended to identify malware, security threats and certain forms of fraud. Marketplace operators must also obtain Apple's authorisation and meet ongoing requirements. Japan has followed a similar route under its Mobile Software Competition Act. With iOS 26.2, Apple introduced alternative app marketplaces and other distribution options in the country, alongside requirements for marketplace authorisation and app notarisation. These changes came in response to the new Japanese law, rather than a voluntary decision by Apple to open its ecosystem. Google's framework differs in one important respect: Android already permits third-party app distribution. Its new programme does not create that right or make registration compulsory. It offers approved marketplaces additional operating system privileges that reduce the friction involved in installing and updating applications. Apple, meanwhile, has introduced alternative distribution in markets where regulation required it to do so, while retaining control over marketplace authorisation and baseline security checks. Both companies therefore retain a role in determining which marketplaces qualify for additional system-level capabilities. The difference lies in the starting point. Apple is opening distribution options in response to regulatory requirements, while Google is formalising an approval system for capabilities on an operating system that already supports sideloading. For Android users, the immediate change will be fewer steps when installing applications from registered marketplaces. Whether this leads to more competition will depend on how many alternative stores enrol, how accessible Google's requirements are to smaller operators and whether developers choose to distribute their applications outside Google Play.

item.title: Jio Platforms Q2 profit rises 13.7% to ₹8,387 crore, revenue up 11.4%
item.description: Jio Platforms reported a 13.7% rise in Q2FY27 net profit to ₹8,389 crore, marking its first quarterly results since the telecom and digital major's record $3.2 billion stock market debut.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / Quarterly Results / Jio Platforms Q2 profit rises 13.7% to ₹8,387 crore, revenue up 11.4%

Jio Platforms Q2 profit rises 13.7% to ₹8,387 crore, revenue up 11.4% JPL IPO broke records across all investor categories; a milestone for the next growth phase: MD Akash Ambani

The company listed on the BSE on October 28, raising Rs 30,188 crore in what was termed India's largest public offering

Gulveen Aulakh New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 11:38 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Jio Platforms Ltd (JPL), the parent company of India’s largest telecom-services provider Reliance Jio, on Friday reported a net profit of ₹8,389 crore for July-September 2026-27 in its first earnings report after its blockbuster market listing earlier this week.     Net profit was up 13.7 per cent from ₹7,379 crore in the same period last financial year.   Revenues rose 11.4 per cent to ₹40,475 crore from ₹36,332 crore the same quarter last year.   In the previous quarter, profits were ₹7,764 crore and revenues ₹39,173 crore. The company raised ₹30,188 crore in what is India’s largest initial public offering. Also Read

RIL's O2C Ebitda jumps 68% on higher fuel cracks and chemical margins

“We were raising ₹30,000 crore-odd, and we saw demand of over ₹7.5 trillion. We saw every investor category broken, starting from QIB (qualified institutional buyers) to small HNI (high net worth), big HNI, retail, and all the various shareholders, employees, all of the categories were broken,” said Akash Ambani, managing director, JPL, at the analyst call following the results.

The top executive at India’s second-largest company by market capitalisation said that JPL’s IPO numbers came at a time when the Indian markets had seen outflows of more than ₹48,000 crore, led by foreign portfolio investors.   “In a market situation like that, (we are) very proud that the people (are) realising (what) business we’ve built ... we put in extremely hard work over the last 10 years to build this business, and we’ll continue to do so,” Ambani noted, adding, the IPO was a new milestone, and that the company would move on from here.   “We believe that you know the value that we can create over the next decade or so is even more than what we have done in our first decade, and we’ll continue to aspire to that perspective,” he said.

Quarterly earnings before interest tax, depreciation and amortisation climbed 16.6 per cent year-on-year to ₹21,879 crore. The 250-basis point rise in margins was driven by revenue growth and operating leverage.   Jio reported average revenue per user (Arpu), a monthly metric of profitability of a telecom services provider, at ₹218.8, marginally up from ₹215.6 in Q1FY27. However, year-on-year, Arpu was up 3.5 per cent, from ₹211.4, on the back of promotional schemes for fixed broadband customers and increased usage.   “We warmly welcome our new shareholders to the Jio Platforms family as we enter a new era as a listed company. This quarter’s results continue to reflect the strength of our 5G network, and the growing reach of our broadband and digital services,” Ambani said in a statement to the exchanges.

The company said in its statement to the stock exchanges that ₹27,500 crore from the net proceeds from the IPO has been used to prepay, in full or in part, the principal amount outstanding of the external commercial borrowing of Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd, a material subsidiary of JPL, and the balance amount would be for general corporate purposes. JPL’s net debt reduced by 78.6 per cent to ₹8,822 crore from ₹41,161 crore in Q2FY26. Debt reduced quarter-on-quarter by 7.5 per cent from ₹9,539 crore in Q1FY27.   Finance costs rose 40.3 per cent to ₹3,009 crore, up from ₹2,145 crore in Q2FY26.

Reliance Jio ended September 2026 with 542.4 million users, including 300 million 5G subscribers. The carrier added 9.1 million subscribers during the quarter.

Jio’s 5G data traffic in the fourth quarter reached 71.3 billion gigabytes, while total voice traffic rose 1.3 per cent to 1.52 trillion minutes. It added 66 million 5G customers over the last 12 months, and 15 million over the past quarter. Customer engagement also remains robust with data consumption at 44.2 GB per month, higher than 38.7 GB per month in the same period last year.   Fixed broadband subscribers as of September 2026 stood at 30 million with about 7.3 million additions over the last 12 months.

Jio AirFiber had over 15.1 million subscribers, driving more than 75 per cent of the fixed broadband additions during the last 12 months, the company said. “Ahead of the curve investment on next generation technologies has been the foundation of Jio’s success over the past decade. We would continue to build our capabilities across satellite communications, 6G intellectual property and AI embedded in our core voice and data services as we create lasting value for all our stakeholders,” Ambani added. He elaborated the company’s strategy, noting that it was unlike a traditional telecom services provider owing largely to its proprietary technology with integrated 4G, 5G stack, unlicensed broadband radio (UBR) and now fixed wireless becoming 50 per cent of its base.

He added that Jio would double down on offers to the enterprise because it would be a major growth opportunity, with India having 350,000 lease lines.    On expanding internationally, Ambani said that the company would be “very selective” about the markets that it would go to.   “We will not be selling our proprietary stacks as a hardware commission … What we imagine the business model here to be is to be actually managed service partner with our customers. It’s not going to be a heavy capex rollout. You won’t see us going and putting up towers and fiber and infrastructure only. But this is something that we think that will be enabled because of the only proprietary stack that we have," he added.

Stating the company’s competitive advantage — owing to full-stack technology across seven layers, deep engineering and proprietary IP contribution — Ambani said Jio had multiple growth engines across mobility, home, enterprise, and international.   “We are the ones that have a clear path of growth and profitability improving with a very strong balance sheet, even before the IPO proceeds come to us,” he added.      ALSO READ:  RIL's O2C Ebitda jumps 68% on higher fuel cracks and chemical margins
